newsitem.title: UK: Strong UK credit data up chances of Aug rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Strong UK credit data up chances of Aug rate rise.

text.p: Another sharp rise in personal credit suggests British consumers are borrowing heavily as well as spending freely, making an August interest rate rise even "This data tells us just how buoyant consumers are feeling. Not only are they spending their windfall cash, but they are happy to borrow more as well," said James Barty, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
He said that added to other recent strong data the Bank of England's monetary policy committee is likely to raise rates by a quarter point at its August 6 and 7 meeting.
"The big headache facing the Bank is how can it slow down the consumer without driving the pound up. We think it will raise rates by a quarter point and hint that it may then pause for a while."
Consumer credit rose by 1.275 billion pounds in June, the highest monthly rise since the monthly series began in 1993.
It rose 1.226 billion pounds in May and the three month growth rate edged up to 19.6 percent in June compared with 17.1 percent in May.

Some analysts had forecast a weak borrowing number for June, speculating that consumers used credit cards to make major purchases in April and May with a view to paying them back with windfall payments due in June.

But the breakdown of the figures by lender showed bank lending posted the only rise in the month -- up by 1.135 billion pounds in June compared with 1.017 billion in May -- suggesting consumers preferred to take on longer-term debt.

"There is little in these figures to suggest that the windfalls received from the conversion of the Alliance & Leicester and the Halifax over the last couple of months have dampened consumers' appetite for credit," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Halifax Plc paid out 18 billion pounds to savers and borrowers in early June, the biggest single windfall payout of the 35 billion pounds or so due this year.

"Consumers are feeling confident enough to take on even more debt despite the recent increases in base rates. These numbers are likely to up the pressure for a further hike in base rates, if not at next month's meeting then soon afterwards," said David.
